content: The guidelines and related materials will be made accessible on the WHO website. Additionally, an executive summary and outreach materials targeting professionals in the health, housing, and urban planning sectors, as well as policymakers and program managers, will be developed and distributed through WHO country offices and their partners. Technical support for adapting and implementing the Housing and Health Guidelines (HHGL) in specific countries will be provided upon request by ministries of health or WHO regional and country offices. Monitoring and evaluation of the HHGL are essential to assess their impact. Health improvements can only be achieved if healthier and safer housing materials, practices, and principles are widely adopted, and if housing is properly maintained and replaced when necessary. Understanding the extent and locations of HHGL implementation will provide insights into their progress and impact. Member States should consider establishing a housing quality surveillance system, similar to public health systems, to monitor housing conditions. One method to evaluate the HHGL's impact is by applying the environmental burden of disease approach to the healthy homes domain. The methodology outlined in the 2011 WHO European Region report on inadequate housing and health effects can be expanded globally and adapted to additional risk factors covered by the HHGL. The implementation toolkit will include guidance on integrating monitoring and evaluation activities into existing data collection processes to minimize additional burdens on statistical offices and reporting bodies. WHO and its partners aim to secure funding to address interventions not reviewed in the HHGL, prioritize research questions to fill identified gaps, and determine effective methods for studying these questions. This includes areas such as access to green spaces, walking and cycling infrastructure, housing interventions to prevent vector-borne diseases, and ventilation improvements. Recommendations will also address multifactorial interventions and the relationship between health and other housing aspects, such as tenure security, residential mobility, structural integrity, and accessibility to public transport and community resources. The immediate housing environment, including streets, recreational facilities, food sources, open spaces, and parks, significantly influences health. Urban and land-use planning are critical public health determinants that require evidence-based guidance. WHO, through the HHGL, can support Member States in reducing health inequities by promoting healthy housing and urban conditions, contributing to global poverty reduction efforts. Guidance will be developed in collaboration with housing, planning, and settlement development sectors, as well as inhabitants and NGOs, to prioritize actions in slums and informal settlements. This guidance will address key health threats, prevention, and promotion practices, and provide advice on implementing the HHGL and related interventions.
